medical.title: Elite athletes don't have better basic eyesight than amateurs, but superior dynamic visual-motor skills
medical.summary: Top athletes do not have sharper eyesight than athletes who compete at lower levels. Their advantage lies in visual skills that have to work at speed. A study of 598 athletes, led by researchers at the Second Faculty of Medicine of Charles University in Prague, found that professionals outperformed nonprofessionals on 6 of 10 visual-motor measures, including depth perception, reaction time and tracking several moving objects at once. On visual clarity and contrast sensitivity, the two groups did not differ.

medical.title: LSD does more than desynchronize the brain—it changes brain rhythms and signal complexity
medical.summary: First synthesized in a laboratory in 1938 by the Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann, lysergic acid diethylamide, better known by its acronym LSD, is one of the most potent and most extensively studied psychedelics.

medical.title: T cell survival protein controls gene activity, offering clues to HIV persistence
medical.summary: A prominent protein on most human cells may be key to unlocking the code that makes humans susceptible to pathogenic bacteria and viruses, including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), according to a new study published in Science Immunology led by researchers at Purdue University and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.

medical.title: Menopause and exercise: Experts share what works
medical.summary: Hot flashes and night sweats tend to dominate conversations about menopause, but some of the most important changes are harder to see—muscle slowly gives way to fat, bones lose density and the body needs fewer calories to get through the day.

medical.title: Caregiving gap grows as women devote more years to aging adults
medical.summary: Women in the United States can expect to provide seven years of care over their lifetimes to aging family members or friends—up from six in 2011, University of Michigan research shows.

medical.title: Functional MRI looks beyond the brain to reveal spinal cord activity
medical.summary: Several EPFL labs are converging around an idea that began as a doctoral researcher's hunch: The spinal cord revealed by functional magnetic resonance imaging might unlock new therapies.

medical.title: Reducing nuclear damage improves heart function and survival in mice
medical.summary: Reducing damage to the nuclei of heart muscle cells improved heart function and extended survival in mice with a form of inherited heart disease, according to a new study led by Cornell researchers. The findings point to new approaches for understanding and potentially treating LMNA-related dilated cardiomyopathy, a disease that leads to heart failure and sudden cardiac death.

medical.title: Started a GLP‑1 drug like Ozempic or Mounjaro? Here's what you need to know about nutrition
medical.summary: Around half a million Australians use GLP-1 medications for diabetes—and when you add people who use them for obesity and weight-related conditions, the total is much higher.

medical.title: The 'activity trap': Fear of losing benefits is stopping some disabled people from exercising
medical.summary: For some people with disabilities, going swimming or attending an exercise class comes with a worry that many others would never consider: Could being seen to be physically active lead to their disability benefits being stopped?

medical.title: Drug could help protect salivary glands during radiation treatment
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Missouri have uncovered a promising way to protect saliva-producing glands from radiation damage that can make it difficult to eat, swallow, sleep and maintain oral hygiene.

medical.title: Tracking maternal depression and bonding may improve early support after childbirth
medical.summary: A Japanese study found that higher postpartum depression scores were associated with greater mother-infant bonding difficulties. Repeated assessments identified varied symptom patterns, including mothers whose bonding difficulties increased during the first three months.

medical.title: CAR T-cell therapy shows lasting improvements in stiff person syndrome, study finds
medical.summary: New research led by the University of Colorado Anschutz is offering hope to people living with stiff person syndrome (SPS), showing that a CAR T-cell therapy may help change the course of the disease, with patients experiencing significant improvements in mobility and overall disability that lasted at least one year after treatment.

medical.title: Hot days linked to fewer births, two new studies find
medical.summary: Hot weather is associated with fewer babies being born in France and Italy, according to two new studies. Each day with an average temperature of 25°C (77 degrees Fahrenheit) or above was linked to about 360 fewer births in France and about 192 fewer in Italy.

medical.title: The hidden role of a cancer treatment target could explain toxic side effects
medical.summary: Wee1 inhibitors are a promising new cancer treatment, but serious side effects threaten their adoption in the clinic. Now, researchers from the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS), the University of Oxford and UCL have discovered a previously unknown role for Wee1 that could explain these effects.

medical.title: Genetic tools point to division of labor among the brain's astrocytes
medical.summary: A new study in Nature by researchers at Baylor College of Medicine answers a long-standing question about astrocytes, star-shaped cells that are the most abundant support cells in the brain and spinal cord.

medical.title: Has your fitness hit a plateau? An expert explains how to track progress and when to change your training plan
medical.summary: If you train regularly, your progress will eventually slow and personal bests will become harder to beat. When this happens, it's tempting to start a completely new training program—but this is usually the wrong move.

medical.title: Smartphones are wrecking teens' sleep, study indicates
medical.summary: Teens who use their phones late into the evening suffer from delays in falling asleep, shorter total sleep time and sleep that's more restless and broken, researchers report in JAMA Pediatrics.

medical.title: Beyond the ice bath: How heat and cold affect recovery
medical.summary: Cold-water immersion is a popular post-workout recovery strategy, but new research suggests it may offer no greater benefit for muscle strength recovery than heat-based methods.

medical.title: Daily blood tests flag potential to stop sepsis antibiotics nearly two days early
medical.summary: A simple daily blood test could help critically ill sepsis patients come off antibiotics sooner, potentially reducing drug overuse and helping tackle the growing threat of antibiotic resistance, new research shows. The study, led by researchers at the University of Manchester and Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, involved 2,760 patients in 41 intensive care units across the U.K. and is published in the journal Anaesthesia.

medical.title: Deep learning using fundus photograph predicts myopia progression
medical.summary: A deep learning algorithm analyzing one fundus photograph can predict progression to moderate or high myopia, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Ophthalmology, held Oct. 9 to 12 in New Orleans.

medical.title: More daily steps over a long period linked to better attention and decision-making
medical.summary: Walking a few extra steps can help your cognitive health go the extra mile. Physical activity has time and again proven its benefits for both mind and body. Regular physical activity, such as walking, is associated with lower blood pressure, while elevated blood pressure has been linked to poorer brain health.

medical.title: Massive study of 460,000 people challenges ultra-processed food cancer fears
medical.summary: A massive study of more than 460,000 Americans found that ultra-processed foods were not associated with increased colorectal cancer risk overall, challenging a widely held assumption. While processed meat was linked to higher cancer incidence, ultra-processed whole grains and dairy products were associated with lower incidence.

medical.title: Too much RNA can starve cells of energy, scientists discover
medical.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected danger lurking inside cells: too much RNA can damage the structures responsible for producing energy. A new study found that excess RNA, including the normally essential messenger RNA (mRNA), can directly disrupt mitochondria without relying on the immune system. The discovery could help explain how viral infections and certain aging-related diseases damage cells.

medical.title: What does a healthy brain look like? It depends on the company you keep
medical.summary: Squishy, wrinkled, weighing about as much as a cantaloupe, the brain may not be much to look at from the outside. Yet with a network of roughly 86 billion neurons, it generates more impulses daily than all the smartphones on the planet combined.

medical.title: Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars
medical.summary: A new study tracking 13 astronauts suggests that the human heart may be surprisingly well equipped for a journey to Mars, especially with regular exercise during spaceflight. Researchers found that astronauts' hearts adapted to months of weightlessness and handled simulated Martian gravity without major problems, offering new hope for future missions to the Red Planet.

science.title: Ultrafast light can control ferromagnetism without relying on heating
science.summary: Despite being known for more mundane uses such as sticking notes to refrigerators or keeping bags shut, magnetization is one of the most fundamental and useful properties of a material. Indeed, it forms the physical basis for storing most of our digital information, encoding the bits used in hard drives, computer memories and credit cards.

science.title: Better data analysis links to stronger marketing and innovation in Thai retail sector
science.summary: A study of 500 Thai retailers has found that businesses with stronger big data analytics capabilities tend to be better at identifying market needs, innovating and executing effective marketing strategies. Moreover, large retailers report higher capability levels than smaller firms, according to research published in the International Journal of Services and Operations Management.

science.title: When a few people break the rules, bad behavior spreads quickly
science.summary: The old saying that one bad apple spoils the barrel suggests that an individual behaving badly can have a negative influence on the entire group. The idea now has some fresh scientific backing.

science.title: Methane emissions in Baltimore show seasonal, daily trends
science.summary: Natural gas leaks are a significant source of methane emissions in cities, but it can be hard to pinpoint exactly where and why they happen. And methane, a potent greenhouse gas that is the main chemical component of natural gas, has been historically undercounted or omitted in emissions estimates, according to a team of atmospheric and climate science researchers in the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences.

science.title: Hubble observations challenge supernova winds' role in cosmic reionization
science.summary: An international team of researchers, including members from the University of Michigan, has revealed surprising results that could rewrite our understanding of a key transition in the early universe.

science.title: Proposed additional ID requirements for voting could disenfranchise more than 1 in 4 Detroit adults
science.summary: More than 1 in 4 Detroiters cannot easily produce up-to-date documentation of their U.S. citizenship that matches their current name, according to a new survey from the University of Michigan's Detroit Metro Area Communities Study, in partnership with Outlier Media.

science.title: Poor ocean conditions leave murrelet chicks exposed to nest predators for longer
science.summary: Less favorable ocean conditions mean marbled murrelet chicks take longer to leave the nest, making them more vulnerable to predation, according to a new study of the Pacific Northwest seabird by Oregon State University scientists.

science.title: Two-in-one tool tracks viral RNA inside live infected cells in real time
science.summary: Viruses are sneaky intruders, hijacking the internal machinery of host cells and replicating out of sight. Understanding these dynamics is the first step to developing effective antiviral strategies that could stop infections, but scientists have largely been left in the dark because there are limited tools to study how viruses move in space and time inside live infected cells, according to Joyce Jose, associate professor of biochemistry and molecular biology at Penn State.

science.title: Africa's bats could survive climate change—if they can find somewhere to live
science.summary: Climate change and changes in the way land is used are the two biggest threats to wildlife because they change the environment in which animals survive and thrive. Knowing how species respond to these pressures is central to planning conservation actions.

science.title: Reindeer grazing changes plant roots in pine forests
science.summary: Reindeer grazing changes the vegetation of northern pine forests below ground as well as above it. In a recent study in Finland, trees and understory vegetation in grazed forests had nearly 30% less shallow-root biomass than those in ungrazed areas. Root structure also changed, which may affect the ability of plants to take up water and nutrients. The research is published in the journal Oikos.

science.title: NASA to Conduct NCAA Flyover, Engage Fans at University of Alabama
science.summary: As part of the agency’s Inspiration Tour, NASA will conduct a flyover at the University of Alabama vs. Texas A&M football game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on Saturday, Oct. 24. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will pilot one of three F-5 fighter jets during the flyover, highlighting NASA’s contributions to aeronautics and the agency’s continued commitment to […]

science.title: Migratory birds spread avian influenza to Greenland's polar bears
science.summary: Migrating birds that breed in the Arctic are spreading avian influenza to polar bears in eastern Greenland, according to a new study that found evidence of infections in bear blood samples acquired from Greenland Inuit subsistence hunters.

science.title: Light-based method could offer first way to detect hypothetical 'mirror life'
science.summary: Scientists have proposed what they believe is the first method for detecting "mirror life"—a hypothetical form of life made from molecular building blocks that are the mirror image of those found naturally on Earth. Researchers at the University of Strathclyde and the Department of Chemistry at Durham University have outlined a new approach that could identify mirror organisms using molecules which emit left- and right-handed light.

science.title: South Korea guides crowd-pulling shark out of canal
science.summary: A shark that has become a viral sensation in South Korea was coaxed out of a canal in which it was stuck, authorities said on Wednesday, as falling temperatures raised concerns for its survival.

science.title: Tracks Along the Longest Drive on Another World
science.summary: Written by Vandi Verma, Chief Engineer for Robotic Operations at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory Oct. 12, 2026 Since the last blog update, Perseverance has achieved a major milestone on Mars. On Sol 2006 (Oct. 11, 2026), its odometer reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles), setting a new record for the farthest distance driven on another celestial […]

science.title: Mirror-image molecules are difficult to separate from their counterparts, but a new catalytic method might be the answer
science.summary: Just like gloves, molecules can have left- and right-handed—or mirror-image—forms. Because the left- and right-handed molecules are still very similar, scientists have had trouble separating them from each other. But a team of researchers in Japan might have found a solution. In their new study, published in Science Advances, the team successfully separated an equal mixture of mirror-image molecules created by replacing hydrogen with deuterium in one form.

science.title: 'Invisible' tweak could help make protein shakes less clumpy
science.summary: Scientists from RMIT University and Riga Technical University in Latvia have shown that static charge left on surfaces can be controlled, which may have big benefits for companies needing to avoid the little zap in production of common household goods. The discovery could even one day help stop powders such as protein, chocolate malt powders and coffee from clumping.

science.title: 'The fishing's terrible': Deforestation devastates Central African river
science.summary: Sitting in his narrow dugout canoe, Jean-Romeo Senguemboli frowned at the meager catch in his nets on the Central African Republic's Mbali River, where experts say deforestation is devastating the fish population.

science.title: UN projections say world is losing ground in fight to curb climate change, faulting US a bit
science.summary: Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year—and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.

science.title: Bending a liquid: Liquid membranes flex 100 times more easily than cell membranes
science.summary: Many structures in biology are bounded by membranes, but not all of them. Droplets of a liquid called a coacervate, which form when oppositely charged molecules come together in water, have attracted attention as models for membraneless compartments inside cells and for "protocells," hypothetical primitive cells that may have preceded modern ones.

science.title: Science on the Space Station with NASA Astronaut Jessica Watkins
science.summary: NASA astronaut and Expedition 75 flight engineer Jessica Watkins works inside the Kibo laboratory module’s Life Science Glovebox on Oct. 9, 2026, safely mixing living cell samples with a bioink and then filling a special cartridge with the cell‑ink mixture. The advanced research operations were part of the InSPA‑Auxilium Bioprinter‑Cell Printing investigation, which explores 3D […]

science.title: Arrival of the Suebi, Alans and Visigoths did not erase deep genetic legacy of Roman Hispania
science.summary: An international study led by the Institute of Evolutionary Biology (IBE, CSIC-UPF) in Barcelona, the Natural Sciences Museum of Barcelona, Harvard University and the University of the Basque Country (EHU) has reconstructed the genetic history of the Iberian Peninsula between the first and eighth centuries A.D. using 243 ancient genomes from 31 archaeological sites.

science.title: Newly identified metabolic pathway helps explain how cold extends lifespan
science.summary: Moderately cold temperatures have proven to effectively extend lifespan and delay age-related decline in animals. However, how cold temperatures trigger these beneficial effects at the molecular level has remained largely unclear.

science.title: Physicists trap and tame single particle of antimatter for months
science.summary: For the first time, Northwestern University physicists have coaxed a single positron—the antimatter counterpart of an electron—into an exquisitely controlled quantum state.

science.title: How many insects are there—and why do we need them?
science.summary: There are an estimated 10 quintillion insects alive on Earth at any given time. That's 10,000,000,000,000,000,000 individual insects. But how many species are there, why do we need them, and what would happen if their numbers continued to fall? Dr. Alex Dittrich, a zoologist at Nottingham Trent University, explains why these small creatures play such a big role in keeping our planet functioning.

environment.title: Governors allied with Flávio Bolsonaro set to lead majority of Brazilian Amazon states
environment.summary: Seven of Brazil’s nine Amazonian states are set to be governed by politicians aligned with far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lucas Berti reported for Mongabay Brasil. On Oct. 25, Brazil will have an electoral face-off between the top two candidates for several races that were not able to secure more than 50% of the vote in […]

environment.title: Inside the ‘unique’ tail of Iran’s spider-tailed horned viper
environment.summary: The Iranian spider-tailed horned viper, a rare snake endemic to western Iran, hunts by holding its body completely still while twitching its tail. Its body camouflages among the rocks of its semi-arid Zagros Mountains habitat, but its bulbous tail with accompanying leg-like scales looks remarkably like a large chunky spider. The snake, Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, uses its […]

environment.title: As sand becomes more valuable, Sierra Leone’s Mahera Coast grows more vulnerable
environment.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — When the tide pulls away from the beach in the agricultural regions in Mahera in Lungi, about 27 kilometers (17 miles) across the sea from the country’s capital, Freetown, the digging commences. Young men shovel sand into cement bags and carry them to a flat open area to pile sand […]

environment.title: New Zealand builds an arsenal of tools to battle a ‘wily’ invasive seaweed
environment.summary: BAY OF ISLANDS, Aotearoa New Zealand — Since an invasive seaweed called caulerpa was discovered in Aotearoa New Zealand in 2021, forming meadows that blanketed parts of the seabed, it’s taken on an almost mythical status among people who spend time in coastal waters. “It’s so wily and so resilient,” Michele Rogalin-Henderson, a doctoral candidate […]

environment.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
environment.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

environment.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
environment.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

environment.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
environment.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

environment.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
environment.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

environment.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
environment.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

environment.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
environment.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.

mix_items.title: Elite athletes don't have better basic eyesight than amateurs, but superior dynamic visual-motor skills
mix_items.summary: Top athletes do not have sharper eyesight than athletes who compete at lower levels. Their advantage lies in visual skills that have to work at speed. A study of 598 athletes, led by researchers at the Second Faculty of Medicine of Charles University in Prague, found that professionals outperformed nonprofessionals on 6 of 10 visual-motor measures, including depth perception, reaction time and tracking several moving objects at once. On visual clarity and contrast sensitivity, the two groups did not differ.

mix_items.title: LSD does more than desynchronize the brain—it changes brain rhythms and signal complexity
mix_items.summary: First synthesized in a laboratory in 1938 by the Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann, lysergic acid diethylamide, better known by its acronym LSD, is one of the most potent and most extensively studied psychedelics.

mix_items.title: Ultrafast light can control ferromagnetism without relying on heating
mix_items.summary: Despite being known for more mundane uses such as sticking notes to refrigerators or keeping bags shut, magnetization is one of the most fundamental and useful properties of a material. Indeed, it forms the physical basis for storing most of our digital information, encoding the bits used in hard drives, computer memories and credit cards.

mix_items.title: Better data analysis links to stronger marketing and innovation in Thai retail sector
mix_items.summary: A study of 500 Thai retailers has found that businesses with stronger big data analytics capabilities tend to be better at identifying market needs, innovating and executing effective marketing strategies. Moreover, large retailers report higher capability levels than smaller firms, according to research published in the International Journal of Services and Operations Management.

mix_items.title: When a few people break the rules, bad behavior spreads quickly
mix_items.summary: The old saying that one bad apple spoils the barrel suggests that an individual behaving badly can have a negative influence on the entire group. The idea now has some fresh scientific backing.

mix_items.title: Methane emissions in Baltimore show seasonal, daily trends
mix_items.summary: Natural gas leaks are a significant source of methane emissions in cities, but it can be hard to pinpoint exactly where and why they happen. And methane, a potent greenhouse gas that is the main chemical component of natural gas, has been historically undercounted or omitted in emissions estimates, according to a team of atmospheric and climate science researchers in the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences.

mix_items.title: Hubble observations challenge supernova winds' role in cosmic reionization
mix_items.summary: An international team of researchers, including members from the University of Michigan, has revealed surprising results that could rewrite our understanding of a key transition in the early universe.

mix_items.title: Proposed additional ID requirements for voting could disenfranchise more than 1 in 4 Detroit adults
mix_items.summary: More than 1 in 4 Detroiters cannot easily produce up-to-date documentation of their U.S. citizenship that matches their current name, according to a new survey from the University of Michigan's Detroit Metro Area Communities Study, in partnership with Outlier Media.

mix_items.title: T cell survival protein controls gene activity, offering clues to HIV persistence
mix_items.summary: A prominent protein on most human cells may be key to unlocking the code that makes humans susceptible to pathogenic bacteria and viruses, including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), according to a new study published in Science Immunology led by researchers at Purdue University and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.

mix_items.title: Menopause and exercise: Experts share what works
mix_items.summary: Hot flashes and night sweats tend to dominate conversations about menopause, but some of the most important changes are harder to see—muscle slowly gives way to fat, bones lose density and the body needs fewer calories to get through the day.

mix_items.title: Poor ocean conditions leave murrelet chicks exposed to nest predators for longer
mix_items.summary: Less favorable ocean conditions mean marbled murrelet chicks take longer to leave the nest, making them more vulnerable to predation, according to a new study of the Pacific Northwest seabird by Oregon State University scientists.

mix_items.title: Two-in-one tool tracks viral RNA inside live infected cells in real time
mix_items.summary: Viruses are sneaky intruders, hijacking the internal machinery of host cells and replicating out of sight. Understanding these dynamics is the first step to developing effective antiviral strategies that could stop infections, but scientists have largely been left in the dark because there are limited tools to study how viruses move in space and time inside live infected cells, according to Joyce Jose, associate professor of biochemistry and molecular biology at Penn State.

mix_items.title: Africa's bats could survive climate change—if they can find somewhere to live
mix_items.summary: Climate change and changes in the way land is used are the two biggest threats to wildlife because they change the environment in which animals survive and thrive. Knowing how species respond to these pressures is central to planning conservation actions.

mix_items.title: Reindeer grazing changes plant roots in pine forests
mix_items.summary: Reindeer grazing changes the vegetation of northern pine forests below ground as well as above it. In a recent study in Finland, trees and understory vegetation in grazed forests had nearly 30% less shallow-root biomass than those in ungrazed areas. Root structure also changed, which may affect the ability of plants to take up water and nutrients. The research is published in the journal Oikos.

mix_items.title: NASA to Conduct NCAA Flyover, Engage Fans at University of Alabama
mix_items.summary: As part of the agency’s Inspiration Tour, NASA will conduct a flyover at the University of Alabama vs. Texas A&M football game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on Saturday, Oct. 24. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will pilot one of three F-5 fighter jets during the flyover, highlighting NASA’s contributions to aeronautics and the agency’s continued commitment to […]

mix_items.title: Caregiving gap grows as women devote more years to aging adults
mix_items.summary: Women in the United States can expect to provide seven years of care over their lifetimes to aging family members or friends—up from six in 2011, University of Michigan research shows.

mix_items.title: Migratory birds spread avian influenza to Greenland's polar bears
mix_items.summary: Migrating birds that breed in the Arctic are spreading avian influenza to polar bears in eastern Greenland, according to a new study that found evidence of infections in bear blood samples acquired from Greenland Inuit subsistence hunters.

mix_items.title: Functional MRI looks beyond the brain to reveal spinal cord activity
mix_items.summary: Several EPFL labs are converging around an idea that began as a doctoral researcher's hunch: The spinal cord revealed by functional magnetic resonance imaging might unlock new therapies.

mix_items.title: Light-based method could offer first way to detect hypothetical 'mirror life'
mix_items.summary: Scientists have proposed what they believe is the first method for detecting "mirror life"—a hypothetical form of life made from molecular building blocks that are the mirror image of those found naturally on Earth. Researchers at the University of Strathclyde and the Department of Chemistry at Durham University have outlined a new approach that could identify mirror organisms using molecules which emit left- and right-handed light.

mix_items.title: Reducing nuclear damage improves heart function and survival in mice
mix_items.summary: Reducing damage to the nuclei of heart muscle cells improved heart function and extended survival in mice with a form of inherited heart disease, according to a new study led by Cornell researchers. The findings point to new approaches for understanding and potentially treating LMNA-related dilated cardiomyopathy, a disease that leads to heart failure and sudden cardiac death.

mix_items.title: South Korea guides crowd-pulling shark out of canal
mix_items.summary: A shark that has become a viral sensation in South Korea was coaxed out of a canal in which it was stuck, authorities said on Wednesday, as falling temperatures raised concerns for its survival.

mix_items.title: Started a GLP‑1 drug like Ozempic or Mounjaro? Here's what you need to know about nutrition
mix_items.summary: Around half a million Australians use GLP-1 medications for diabetes—and when you add people who use them for obesity and weight-related conditions, the total is much higher.

mix_items.title: Mirror-image molecules are difficult to separate from their counterparts, but a new catalytic method might be the answer
mix_items.summary: Just like gloves, molecules can have left- and right-handed—or mirror-image—forms. Because the left- and right-handed molecules are still very similar, scientists have had trouble separating them from each other. But a team of researchers in Japan might have found a solution. In their new study, published in Science Advances, the team successfully separated an equal mixture of mirror-image molecules created by replacing hydrogen with deuterium in one form.

mix_items.title: 'Invisible' tweak could help make protein shakes less clumpy
mix_items.summary: Scientists from RMIT University and Riga Technical University in Latvia have shown that static charge left on surfaces can be controlled, which may have big benefits for companies needing to avoid the little zap in production of common household goods. The discovery could even one day help stop powders such as protein, chocolate malt powders and coffee from clumping.

mix_items.title: The 'activity trap': Fear of losing benefits is stopping some disabled people from exercising
mix_items.summary: For some people with disabilities, going swimming or attending an exercise class comes with a worry that many others would never consider: Could being seen to be physically active lead to their disability benefits being stopped?

mix_items.title: 'The fishing's terrible': Deforestation devastates Central African river
mix_items.summary: Sitting in his narrow dugout canoe, Jean-Romeo Senguemboli frowned at the meager catch in his nets on the Central African Republic's Mbali River, where experts say deforestation is devastating the fish population.

mix_items.title: Drug could help protect salivary glands during radiation treatment
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Missouri have uncovered a promising way to protect saliva-producing glands from radiation damage that can make it difficult to eat, swallow, sleep and maintain oral hygiene.

mix_items.title: UN projections say world is losing ground in fight to curb climate change, faulting US a bit
mix_items.summary: Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year—and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.

mix_items.title: Tracking maternal depression and bonding may improve early support after childbirth
mix_items.summary: A Japanese study found that higher postpartum depression scores were associated with greater mother-infant bonding difficulties. Repeated assessments identified varied symptom patterns, including mothers whose bonding difficulties increased during the first three months.

mix_items.title: Bending a liquid: Liquid membranes flex 100 times more easily than cell membranes
mix_items.summary: Many structures in biology are bounded by membranes, but not all of them. Droplets of a liquid called a coacervate, which form when oppositely charged molecules come together in water, have attracted attention as models for membraneless compartments inside cells and for "protocells," hypothetical primitive cells that may have preceded modern ones.

mix_items.title: CAR T-cell therapy shows lasting improvements in stiff person syndrome, study finds
mix_items.summary: New research led by the University of Colorado Anschutz is offering hope to people living with stiff person syndrome (SPS), showing that a CAR T-cell therapy may help change the course of the disease, with patients experiencing significant improvements in mobility and overall disability that lasted at least one year after treatment.

mix_items.summary: NASA astronaut and Expedition 75 flight engineer Jessica Watkins works inside the Kibo laboratory module’s Life Science Glovebox on Oct. 9, 2026, safely mixing living cell samples with a bioink and then filling a special cartridge with the cell‑ink mixture. The advanced research operations were part of the InSPA‑Auxilium Bioprinter‑Cell Printing investigation, which explores 3D […]

mix_items.title: Hot days linked to fewer births, two new studies find
mix_items.summary: Hot weather is associated with fewer babies being born in France and Italy, according to two new studies. Each day with an average temperature of 25°C (77 degrees Fahrenheit) or above was linked to about 360 fewer births in France and about 192 fewer in Italy.

mix_items.title: Arrival of the Suebi, Alans and Visigoths did not erase deep genetic legacy of Roman Hispania
mix_items.summary: An international study led by the Institute of Evolutionary Biology (IBE, CSIC-UPF) in Barcelona, the Natural Sciences Museum of Barcelona, Harvard University and the University of the Basque Country (EHU) has reconstructed the genetic history of the Iberian Peninsula between the first and eighth centuries A.D. using 243 ancient genomes from 31 archaeological sites.

mix_items.title: Newly identified metabolic pathway helps explain how cold extends lifespan
mix_items.summary: Moderately cold temperatures have proven to effectively extend lifespan and delay age-related decline in animals. However, how cold temperatures trigger these beneficial effects at the molecular level has remained largely unclear.

mix_items.title: The hidden role of a cancer treatment target could explain toxic side effects
mix_items.summary: Wee1 inhibitors are a promising new cancer treatment, but serious side effects threaten their adoption in the clinic. Now, researchers from the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS), the University of Oxford and UCL have discovered a previously unknown role for Wee1 that could explain these effects.

mix_items.title: Physicists trap and tame single particle of antimatter for months
mix_items.summary: For the first time, Northwestern University physicists have coaxed a single positron—the antimatter counterpart of an electron—into an exquisitely controlled quantum state.

mix_items.title: Genetic tools point to division of labor among the brain's astrocytes
mix_items.summary: A new study in Nature by researchers at Baylor College of Medicine answers a long-standing question about astrocytes, star-shaped cells that are the most abundant support cells in the brain and spinal cord.

mix_items.title: How many insects are there—and why do we need them?
mix_items.summary: There are an estimated 10 quintillion insects alive on Earth at any given time. That's 10,000,000,000,000,000,000 individual insects. But how many species are there, why do we need them, and what would happen if their numbers continued to fall? Dr. Alex Dittrich, a zoologist at Nottingham Trent University, explains why these small creatures play such a big role in keeping our planet functioning.

mix_items.title: Has your fitness hit a plateau? An expert explains how to track progress and when to change your training plan
mix_items.summary: If you train regularly, your progress will eventually slow and personal bests will become harder to beat. When this happens, it's tempting to start a completely new training program—but this is usually the wrong move.

mix_items.title: Smartphones are wrecking teens' sleep, study indicates
mix_items.summary: Teens who use their phones late into the evening suffer from delays in falling asleep, shorter total sleep time and sleep that's more restless and broken, researchers report in JAMA Pediatrics.

mix_items.title: Beyond the ice bath: How heat and cold affect recovery
mix_items.summary: Cold-water immersion is a popular post-workout recovery strategy, but new research suggests it may offer no greater benefit for muscle strength recovery than heat-based methods.

mix_items.title: Daily blood tests flag potential to stop sepsis antibiotics nearly two days early
mix_items.summary: A simple daily blood test could help critically ill sepsis patients come off antibiotics sooner, potentially reducing drug overuse and helping tackle the growing threat of antibiotic resistance, new research shows. The study, led by researchers at the University of Manchester and Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, involved 2,760 patients in 41 intensive care units across the U.K. and is published in the journal Anaesthesia.

mix_items.title: Deep learning using fundus photograph predicts myopia progression
mix_items.summary: A deep learning algorithm analyzing one fundus photograph can predict progression to moderate or high myopia, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Ophthalmology, held Oct. 9 to 12 in New Orleans.

mix_items.title: More daily steps over a long period linked to better attention and decision-making
mix_items.summary: Walking a few extra steps can help your cognitive health go the extra mile. Physical activity has time and again proven its benefits for both mind and body. Regular physical activity, such as walking, is associated with lower blood pressure, while elevated blood pressure has been linked to poorer brain health.

mix_items.title: Massive study of 460,000 people challenges ultra-processed food cancer fears
mix_items.summary: A massive study of more than 460,000 Americans found that ultra-processed foods were not associated with increased colorectal cancer risk overall, challenging a widely held assumption. While processed meat was linked to higher cancer incidence, ultra-processed whole grains and dairy products were associated with lower incidence.

mix_items.title: Too much RNA can starve cells of energy, scientists discover
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected danger lurking inside cells: too much RNA can damage the structures responsible for producing energy. A new study found that excess RNA, including the normally essential messenger RNA (mRNA), can directly disrupt mitochondria without relying on the immune system. The discovery could help explain how viral infections and certain aging-related diseases damage cells.

mix_items.title: What does a healthy brain look like? It depends on the company you keep
mix_items.summary: Squishy, wrinkled, weighing about as much as a cantaloupe, the brain may not be much to look at from the outside. Yet with a network of roughly 86 billion neurons, it generates more impulses daily than all the smartphones on the planet combined.

mix_items.title: Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars
mix_items.summary: A new study tracking 13 astronauts suggests that the human heart may be surprisingly well equipped for a journey to Mars, especially with regular exercise during spaceflight. Researchers found that astronauts' hearts adapted to months of weightlessness and handled simulated Martian gravity without major problems, offering new hope for future missions to the Red Planet.

mix_items.title: Governors allied with Flávio Bolsonaro set to lead majority of Brazilian Amazon states
mix_items.summary: Seven of Brazil’s nine Amazonian states are set to be governed by politicians aligned with far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lucas Berti reported for Mongabay Brasil. On Oct. 25, Brazil will have an electoral face-off between the top two candidates for several races that were not able to secure more than 50% of the vote in […]

mix_items.title: Inside the ‘unique’ tail of Iran’s spider-tailed horned viper
mix_items.summary: The Iranian spider-tailed horned viper, a rare snake endemic to western Iran, hunts by holding its body completely still while twitching its tail. Its body camouflages among the rocks of its semi-arid Zagros Mountains habitat, but its bulbous tail with accompanying leg-like scales looks remarkably like a large chunky spider. The snake, Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, uses its […]

mix_items.title: As sand becomes more valuable, Sierra Leone’s Mahera Coast grows more vulnerable
mix_items.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — When the tide pulls away from the beach in the agricultural regions in Mahera in Lungi, about 27 kilometers (17 miles) across the sea from the country’s capital, Freetown, the digging commences. Young men shovel sand into cement bags and carry them to a flat open area to pile sand […]

mix_items.title: New Zealand builds an arsenal of tools to battle a ‘wily’ invasive seaweed

mix_items.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
mix_items.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

mix_items.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
mix_items.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

mix_items.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
mix_items.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

mix_items.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
mix_items.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

mix_items.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
mix_items.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

mix_items.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.
